title: My takeaways after 3 months of using AI for my video game
author: Affro_riffo
selftext:
In August 2026, I started making my first “real” game. I have a background in game design, some graphic skills (2D artwork, UI) and almost no dev skills (C# basics). So AI looked like a way to get started, more out of opportunism and curiosity than laziness (at least at first). 

In the anti vs. pro-AI fight, I have mixed feelings, and that’s why I’m sharing this post. I’m tired of people jumping down your throat the second you say you use AI, because to me, you can make a personal, crafted game while still using it. But at the same time, it makes me sad to see some people releasing games made entirely with AI, with zero depth or personality and shitty designs, and thinking they’re revolutionizing the game industry. I really think there’s a sweet spot between both, so here are my takeaways: 

1. **AI is a decision accelerator:** What impressed me most is being able to produce a playable sequence in just a few prompts. Anyone who’s done game design knows this fact: every design works on paper. But the real test is the gameplay. With AI, you can test almost everything right away, and it really helps you validate or throw out an idea in a few hours, when it would have taken days or even weeks to develop (at least for me, given my dev level). 
2. **AI can’t make a complete game:** A gameplay sequence isn’t a game, and once the wow effect is gone, all you’ve got is a hollow shell. If you ask it to build one or more systems with just vague prompts, you’ll get no progression, no coherence between mechanics, no flow, no game feel. Nothing. You have to make all those decisions yourself. AI can make them for you, but nothing good will come out of it and nothing will feel coherent together. It’s a great prototyping tool, but honestly, it stops there. AI can’t turn a set of mechanics into one experience. So yes, you can create a whole game with AI, but no, you won’t create a good game. 
3. **AI doesn’t have good ideas:** In a way, it reassured me the most. It can help you structure your ideas or push them a bit further, but it never comes up with an idea ready to be used, or even surprising. Whether it’s mechanics or, in my case, dialogue and story, it’s honestly quite bad and very “déjà vu”. I still use it a bit for brainstorming (even crappy answers sometimes lead me to another idea), but that’s it.
4. **AI is a good tool for structuring your production:** In the end, this is where it helps me the most. Example: my game has a lot of NPCs, and with AI I built a spreadsheet that centralizes all their content and plugs into the engine in a few clicks. That file and all its formulas would have taken me weeks to make myself. Now I can focus purely on the content. I also have an agent with all my design docs in context that I can use as an interactive game bible. If I have a question about my design, it can answer it, which saves me a ton of back-and-forth between all my files. 
5. **AI is a dev beast (that's a lie):** <!>Disclaimer - I’m not a developer, so maybe what I’m saying here is not accurate. <!> The crazy thing is that the generated code is super functional. It actually works great! But the bad side is that it doesn’t look optimized at all, and personally I’m lost every time I open a script, because I don’t really understand what it’s for. And iteration after iteration, AI has created a thousand different files that work together, I just don’t know how. I’m at the point where I don’t dare open some files, even to fix a tiny thing. It’s overcomplicated to understand, and that’s something you absolutely want to avoid. That’s why I can’t even imagine making a full game entirely with AI: in terms of complexity, performance, debugging… I can’t imagine what 100% AI game code looks like after 6-12 months of work by a non-developer. So for me it’s very clear: once prototyping is done, I’ll start everything over from scratch (in a few weeks) and implement my own crafted features, script by script. I’ll probably still use AI for isolated things, but never to build a whole feature with it.
6. **AI is very addictive:** This is what worries me the most. You quickly get into the habit of using it for everything, and you have to constantly fight your own laziness. It’s a bit like a drug: you know the downsides, but the hit is still tempting and super satisfying in the moment. Then comes the comedown, where you either realize the output isn’t great, feel awful (hello, impostor syndrome), or even panic at the slightest challenge. The tool is so easy to access, and it takes a lot of willpower not to take a “shot” (in my case at least, I guess it depends on your personality).
7. **Don't use AI for visual and audio assets:** I tried only a few times, and not a single AI creation (visual or audio) ever satisfied me. Seriously, there are so many free or paid assets online that do the job so much better, at least for a prototype. At most, AI can create placeholders, but even there, I’ve always found something better elsewhere. I’ve always loved drawing and cared about art, so I’d rather create everything myself or ask for help from people who are skilled at it. A video game is mainly visuals and sound: standing out and having a real style is essential. Not to mention all the backlash risk that comes with using AI art (if we can even call it that…). It would be a shame for all your work to get trashed just because you used AI assets. But from a player’s point of view, I guess it’s legit. And we can see it the other way: using slop assets can be seen as spitting on your own work, don’t you think? 

**Conclusion** 

AI feels essential to me today, but it can turn against you very fast. You produce so quickly, which is great, but you can easily drown in your own production and slowly lose both the vision and the joy of creating things yourself. I’ll keep using it for a few more weeks to prototype my loops, then switch to homemade dev. That being said, I have to admit I’d never have gotten this far, this fast, without AI. I’d even say it gave me the confidence to start, by protecting me from the “dev wall” on my very first scripts. Important note: a real, professional developer will join the project (essential in my situation). I’ll keep using AI for project management, my game bible, and probably for admin stuff and planning the launch/marketing strategy. 

I guess that’s it. Maybe I don’t realize AI has already fucked my mind, and some of you will maybe hate me and say I’m just justifying my use of AI to convince myself I’m still a creator. Anyway, I guess I’m not the only one with this mindset about this tool. Or am I?

comments.author: Burning_magic
comments.body:
As someone who coded pre AI, AI right now is 100% capable of handling all your scripting. You just need to make sure to modularise your scripts/ask ai to do it.

As for optimisation, I would recommend you spend 2-3 weeks watching yt videos on game engine fundamentals. You dont need to code, but you need to know theory stuff like cpu vs gpu, what to optimise and when. (This is not required for a 2d game, only 3d)

As for other stuff, ai is ok at basic animations. Its horrible at modelling/texturing and ok for deterministic shaders, bad for stylised shaders.

replies.author: Purple-Measurement47
replies.body:
As someone who does both full time, this is not super accurate. Every model I’ve used you still have to have a decent pseudoscript, and you have to be able to check the script against it. If you just ask it to script things, it’ll make some really bad decisions. 

Optimization is far more than just theory that’s needed for game dev, and is *absolutely* needed for 2D games. It is not needed for basic platformers. In fact, some of my most important optimizations have been for 2D games. It doesn’t matter which dimension you’re working in, it matters what your project is. Basic scene with one light source, a couple dozen models/sprites and animations? No worries. Thousands of agents calculating actions, pathfinding, etc? Absolutely needed. 

placeholder animations are decent, shaders can be pretty great

replies.author: Burning_magic
replies.body:
Oh, at least 2d games I was thinking of was something like balatro where I doubt you need much optimisation. If its those 1 million items 2d games (is there even any lol) then yea you need. I dont think vampire survivors is heavy even with minimal optimisation.

Hmm at least for me once you modularise it into nodes, its much easier to manage with each nodes script being less than 2k loc.

replies.author: Purple-Measurement47
replies.body: Vampire Survivors and Balatro both need pretty solid optimizations if you don’t want to burn out the players computer

comments.author: yawnlikeseggs
comments.body:
Definitely wrong about the limits (I can tell you’re not a software engineer or developer).

It takes time to understand project workflows, what software stack to use for development and so on.  However, if you know these things prior to starting a project (a game), ai is capable of handling 100% of the tasks.  

Anti / pro ai is a pointless argument for people not in the field.  99% of software and game devs use ai at some level.  Frontier models are getting better and better… if a dev isn’t using ai tools… I would question if they’re a dev / understand technology / what they think that they do better.

comments.author: WhiteBlackBlueGreen
comments.body:
You could use AI for nice and consistent visual assets but it would be a lot of work, and would still be less flexible than human-made art. Most people aren't willing to go through a whole lot of effort for it. 

One thing I've had success with though is using ai to make a procedural character creation tool. The generated characters look pretty good and AI is capable of adding basic features like hair styles, facial hair, face types, and bodies (it struggles with clothing in my experience)

comments.author: eduo
comments.body:
Great post. A couple comments

AI is not good at art but it’s good at explaining theory and helping figure out usability and layouts. What it comes with is functional but ugly or is flashy but inviable. It can also help a lot with learning industry terms you might need later on for cases and UIs you’re implementing got the first time, which makes documenting yourself easier. 

AI is limited by the technology it makes things in. Claude uses html and css. ChatGPT uses an image generator. Keep this in mind when evaluating mockups and proposals. 

If your chosen art style can support it, consider going vectorial or using true pixel art. A very small investment in understanding these helps a lot optimizing your game. As an old fart I get conniptions when I see “pixel art” that is several MB because it’s hi def art made to look like pixels. The one advantage of using tiny images completely wasted. Remember that each card in Balatro is just 93 pixels hugh by 69 wide. That’s barely 45KB for a full poker deck and less than one megabyte for all cards in the game and most assets added to the pile. AI can’t make it for you but can help you get there even down to the necessary automations. 

AI know more about gaming theory than you. It knows nothing  about playing but can execute simulators for many types of gameplays that will be fundamental in finding balance. Monte Carlo simulations, A/B testing, self-playing by the AI opponents, Minimax, MCTS, Nash equilibrium, CFR, reinforcement learning, Elo, Trueskill, etc 

Have the AI create tools to help you do the things you do better. If you’re making a deck have it build a card tool that lets you try layouts and art. If you use sounds have it build a tool that makes it easy to iterate quickly between sounds and sound sets. Have it visually show automated play with a sidebar showing decisions after telling it which constraints to apply. 

Use two different models and ask one to evaluate the other’s decisions. Especially regarding UI and UX. Have one do a mockup from the other’s descriptions. Etc.

Use it for translations but check the originals first and insist on language and conciseness. Have it keep track of progress and prune files archiving closed decisions from time to time

comments.author: daddy_reloaded
comments.body:
I tend to post only positive comments, but seriously, 3 months of Dev and you think you can fix your opinion?
For example, saying that ai doesn't have good ideas... Do you realise that it has already found mathematical proof of undemonstrable math problems? You should probably think twice... Bad hands doesn't make a bad tool...

Also, not using ai for visual and audio? I am ok with that if you have personal beliefs, but technically, did you ever try suno ou things like that ? 

One drawback I found for ai (to finish with a non pro ai sentence) is that sometimes I feel much more efficient by thinking alone but it is more and more difficult to escape from the ai efficient easyness...

replies.author: eduo
replies.body:
This response sounds unnecessarily antagonistic while missing a few points. 

Your example of why AI could have good ideas because it’s found solutions about mathematical problems hints at you not understanding how LLMs work and how math problems like these are solved. If you did you’d understand an LLM is particularly optimized for finding patterns in known data and that is the exact opposite of “having a good idea”. 

You’re attacking a poster that is knowledgeably pro AI sharing their experience with generic and unbased pro AI arguments obviously not based on experience. Seems unnecessary.

replies.author: daddy_reloaded
replies.body:
I have to disagree. Actually I took the math example because it's my expertise field. Also, maths is a very good example in general to asses creativity because it can be objectively evaluate (to some extent).
Commercial models have already been used to found new demonstrations, and recently anthropic has published a very interesting improvement about zeta Riemann with a Claude version that we will be available soon in fable.

So saying that ai can have a good ideas "in any way" is not an accurate statement.

But you are also right, my post was unnecessary aggressive.

replies.author: eduo
replies.body:
We define “have good ideas” in this context as being creative. You’re defining it as collating lots of experience into extrapolations. 

Unless “having good ideas” in the context of game development meant “show me something I can’t see but it’s there based on all the known data”, in which case it’s a different definition. 

A post recently used LLMs to find “holes” in game development trends using existing data to map a space and then statistics to find untapped holes. It then used LLM to suggest games based on those holes. 

That was a clever use of LLM and statistics but that wasn’t the LLM having good ideas either. 

Perhaps the issue is that we’re treating subjective definitions as absolute.

comments.author: ledniv
comments.body:
I agree with a lot of this, especially the part about AI creating code that works but slowly becomes impossible to understand. Where I came to a different conclusion is that I do not think the solution is to stop using AI after prototyping. The problem is that the AI needs architectural rules before it starts generating features. Otherwise every prompt can introduce a new pattern, another abstraction, another manager, another event system, and eventually you get exactly the thousand file codebase you described.

What has worked much better for me is defining the architecture once, then making the AI follow it. Gameplay state lives in data, gameplay logic is kept separate from presentation, hot data is processed in arrays, memory is allocated deliberately, and the AI is told where new features are allowed to put their data and logic. I have used this approach to build complete games with AI, including much larger projects, without throwing the codebase away afterward.

I turned those rules into a free coding skill so the agent can follow them automatically and review its own code for violations:

[https://github.com/Data-Oriented-Design-for-Games/data-oriented-design](https://github.com/Data-Oriented-Design-for-Games/data-oriented-design)

Small plug: the architecture behind the skill is what I cover in *High Performance Unity Game Development with Data Oriented Design*:

[https://www.manning.com/books/high-performance-unity-game-development](https://www.manning.com/books/high-performance-unity-game-development)

comments.author: drahgon
comments.body: No joke. It has terrible ideas. And I feel like also it can’t really come up with novel ideas. That’s honestly it’s the biggest weakness and I think if it could crack that it would really bring it to another frontier. That would be kind of dangerous. And I think it’s the last frontier that separates the humans from AI at this point if you asked me.

For 6 don't worry. The part that matters the most, the gamefeel, should be made manually. For everything else - it's not a lazyness, it's a timesaver. If you wanna study the engine and code, do it on studying project, not on what is your soul project

The point is, AI output with human post processing can achieve something, that looks good and optimized well. AI art is a skill too, someone have it better 

Overall you're correct. I hope more people would devote all their creativity to make a good AI game, and not just one shot astra claude and call it a day
